division-and-remainder.why: int / int is integer division and drops the fraction; one double operand makes it floating-point. In Java the remainder takes the sign of the left operand, so -7 % 3 is -1, not 2.

overflow.why: big + 1 is int arithmetic and wraps around to Integer.MIN_VALUE without any error. Adding 1L makes the whole expression long, which has room for the result.

cast-truncates.why: Casting a double to int truncates toward zero: the fraction is simply dropped, so -3.99 becomes -3 (not -4, which rounding down would give). Use Math.floor or Math.round when you mean those.

char-arithmetic.why: char is a 16-bit number. c += 2 stores the result back as a char ('C'), but 'A' + 2 on its own is int arithmetic, so println gets the int 67.

integer-equality.why: == on objects compares references. It happens to work for small values (-128 to 127 are cached) and then fails for larger ones, which makes it a nasty bug. equals compares the values.

safe-midpoint.why: (lo + hi) / 2 can overflow when the sum passes Integer.MAX_VALUE. lo + (hi - lo) / 2 never computes anything larger than hi.

floating-point.why: 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 have no exact binary representation, so the sum is 0.30000000000000004. Compare doubles within a tolerance, and keep money in integer cents.

char-unsigned.why: 'A' is 65; adding an int promotes the char to int, giving 66. Cast back with (char) to get 'B'.
